newsitem.title: UK: US banker in key role at Britain's NatWest.
newsitem.headline: US banker in key role at Britain's NatWest.

text.p: Sweeping changes at National Westminster Bank on Friday brought a highly regarded American to a key position in one of Britain's largest financial institutions.

NatWest announced the appointment of Konrad "Chip" Kruger as chief executive of NatWest Markets, part of a strategic review promised this year after a 90-million-pound ($147 million) options-related loss was revealed at the subsidiary.

Kruger, a 44-year-old debt specialist with an ivy-league degree, would barely have been known in London's financial circles before last year. He was a senior executive at U.S. bond trading house Greenwich Capital Markets.
NatWest had acquired Greenwich in 1996 and bankers in London said the latest changes reflect the power that Greenwich now wields within the British bank.
"It's the classic reverse takeover -- Goliath taking over David, but David coming out on top," said one banker.
Kruger and other NatWest executives who featured in the restructuring were not available for interviews on Friday. The bank is due to release interim profit results next week.
Kruger is currently co-chief executive of NatWest Market's Global Debt Markets division and was co-president and co-chief executive of Greenwich.
Greenwich has a reputation, both in New York and London, as a tough trading firm, and its influence on NatWest is likely to be immense, bankers said.
"NatWest, a sleepy old UK clearing house, is going to be knocked into the new millennium by an aggressive U.S. trading house," said one.
Banking sources compare NatWest's takeover of the Connecticut-based trading and derivatives specialist to Swiss Bank Corp's acquisition of Chicago-based O'Connor Associates between 1989 and 1992.
Former O'Connor executives are calling the shots at SBC, and that is reflected in the Swiss bank's market strategy, industry sources said.
"SBC is becoming completely O'Connorised -- the move towards derivatives and structured transactions has been driven by O'Connor," said one.

Kruger joined Greenwich Capital Markets in 1983 from Chemical Bank. Prior to Friday, he was responsible for corporate lending, fixed income, derivatives and futures at NatWest. Now he will oversee much of the investment banking side of the business.
An MBA graduate from Dartmouth College, he is described by London banking sources as a smooth-talking American, but not brash.
"He is what you would expect of a Greenwich employee," said one industry source.

British banks have been characterised in the past as being less savvy with complicated derivatives products than their U.S. rivals. The collapse of the British merchant bank Barings, as well as the options loss at NatWest, were two of the more notable events that contributed to this image.

NatWest said it was removing the treasury, foreign exchange, interest rate trading, money market and currency options functions from NatWest Markets and putting them in a new Global Financial Markets sector under NatWest executive Stephan Harris.
Global Financial Markets is currently part of NatWest Markets.
Harris, 50, is already chief executive of Global Financial Markets and also group treasurer of the NatWest Group.
NatWest also said its group chief executive, Derek Wanless, who has been running NatWest Markets since the resignation of its former head Martin Owen, will become chairman of NatWest Markets.
